pages.summary: The sum of the diagonal of a square matrix.
body: The trace is also the sum of the eigenvalues, and `trace(A*B)` equals `trace(B*A)`.

examples.title: The diagonal's sum, and the eigenvalues'

pages.summary: The norm of each column of a matrix, or along another dimension.
body: The 2-norm (length) of each column by default; `p` gives another norm (1, Inf, or any positive number) and `dim` the direction: 2 for the norm of each row.

examples.title: Columns and rows
examples.code:
A = [3 -2; 4 0; 0 6];
vecnorm(A)
vecnorm(A, 1)
vecnorm(A, 2, 2)

pages.summary: The condition number of a matrix: how much solving with it can magnify errors.
body: The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value (the 2-norm), or `norm(A, p)*norm(inv(A), p)` for p = 1, Inf or `'fro'`. A condition number near 10^k means about k digits may be lost when solving `A*x = b`; a singular matrix has `Inf`.
syntax: In the 1-, Inf- or Frobenius norm.

examples.title: Two nearly parallel equations
examples.intro: A change of 0.001 in the right-hand side moves the solution by 2: about four of the digits are lost, as the condition number says.

examples.title: Hilbert matrices grow ill-conditioned fast

pages.summary: Estimates of the condition number in the 1-norm: its reciprocal (`rcond`) and the number itself (`condest`).
body: Cheaper than `cond`, which needs the singular values. `rcond` is near 1 for a well-conditioned matrix and near `eps` (or 0) for a nearly singular one; `condest` works on large sparse matrices too, without forming the inverse.

examples.title: The estimates beside the exact numbers
A singular matrix
examples.code: rcond(magic(4))

pages.summary: Estimates of a matrix's 2-norm and 1-norm.
body: For a large sparse matrix, where `norm` would need the singular values: `normest` runs the power method on `A'*A` until the estimate settles within `tol` (1e-6); `normest1` uses a block method that looks at a few columns at a time.
syntax: Within a tolerance, with the number of iterations.
With `t` columns, and a vector `v` with `w = A*v` that attains it.

examples.title: A sparse matrix's norms
examples.code:
rng default
A = sprand(300, 300, 0.02);
[normest(A) norm(full(A))]
[normest1(A) norm(A, 1)]

pages.summary: A few eigenvalues of a large (often sparse) matrix: the largest in magnitude by default.
body: When only some eigenvalues are wanted, `eigs` finds them by an iterative (Krylov) method without the cost of `eig` on the whole matrix. `sigma` says which: `'smallestabs'` (by factoring the matrix), `'largestreal'` and the like, or a number for those nearest it. With a matrix `B`, the generalized problem `A*v = lambda*B*v`; with a function handle, a matrix given only by what it does to a vector.
syntax: Others: `'smallestabs'`, `'largestreal'`, `'smallestreal'`, ... or the `k` nearest a number.
With the eigenvectors; `flag` 0 when all converged.
Of an `n`-by-`n` matrix given as a function.

examples.title: The lowest modes of a sparse Laplacian
examples.intro: The 400-by-400 five-point Laplacian on a 20-by-20 grid has eigenvalues 4 - 2cos(iπ/21) - 2cos(jπ/21).

examples.title: Vectors, and how well they satisfy A*V = V*D

pages.summary: A few singular values of a large matrix: the largest by default.
body: The partial counterpart of `svd`: the `k` largest singular values (or the smallest, or those nearest a number), with their vectors if asked.
syntax: `'smallest'`, `'smallestnz'` (the smallest not zero) or those nearest a number.

examples.title: The largest three, against the full decomposition

pages.summary: The Cholesky factorization of a symmetric positive definite matrix: A = R'*R.
body: `R` is upper triangular (`L = chol(A, 'lower')` gives `A = L*L'`). It takes half the work of LU and needs no pivoting, and it exists only when the matrix is positive definite: with two outputs, `p` is 0 when it is and otherwise the column where it failed, so `chol` is also the quickest test of positive definiteness.
syntax: `p` 0 when `A` is positive definite (no error otherwise).

examples.title: Samples with a given covariance
examples.intro: If z has independent standard normal entries, L*z has covariance L*L'.

pages.summary: The Schur decomposition A = U*T*U', its reordering, and the real form turned complex.
body: `U` is unitary and `T` upper triangular with the eigenvalues on its diagonal; for a real matrix the real form keeps complex pairs as 2-by-2 blocks on the diagonal (quasi-triangular), and `'complex'` or `rsf2csf` makes it triangular. Unlike the eigenvector matrix, `U` is always well conditioned. `ordschur` reorders `U` and `T` so the eigenvalues picked by `select` (true at their positions on `T`'s diagonal) come first.
syntax: A real Schur form made complex triangular.

examples.title: The form and its eigenvalues
The negative eigenvalue moved first
A rotation: real blocks, then complex

pages.summary: The generalized Schur (QZ) factorization of a pair of matrices, its reordering, and eigenvalues in diagonal order.
body: For the generalized problem `A*v = lambda*B*v`: `Q*A*Z = AA` and `Q*B*Z = BB` with `AA` and `BB` upper triangular (quasi-triangular with `'real'`), and the eigenvalues are `diag(AA)./diag(BB)`; `B` may be singular, which gives infinite eigenvalues. `ordqz` moves chosen eigenvalues first: by a logical `select`, or `'lhp'`, `'rhp'` (left or right half-plane), `'udi'`, `'udo'` (inside or outside the unit disk). `ordeig` gives the eigenvalues of a (quasi-)triangular form in the order of its diagonal.
syntax: [AA, BB, Q, Z, V, W] = qz(A, B, 'real')
Real, with the right and left eigenvectors.
[AAS, BBS, QS, ZS] = ordqz(AA, BB, Q, Z, keyword)
A Schur form's eigenvalues, in order.
A QZ form's eigenvalues, in order.

examples.title: The pair's eigenvalues
Eigenvalues outside the unit disk first

pages.summary: The Hessenberg form of a matrix: A = P*H*P', zero below the first subdiagonal.
body: A unitary similarity, so `H` keeps `A`'s eigenvalues; it is the first step of the eigenvalue algorithms, and a symmetric matrix becomes tridiagonal.

examples.title: A matrix brought to Hessenberg form

pages.summary: The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse.
body: Defined for any matrix, square or not, singular or not, through the singular values: those above `tol` are inverted, the rest set to zero. `pinv(A)*b` is the least-squares solution with the smallest norm; for an invertible matrix `pinv` is `inv`.
syntax: With singular values at or below `tol` treated as zero.

pages.summary: Orthonormal bases of a matrix's null space and range.
body: `null(A)` has a column for each independent `x` with `A*x = 0`; `orth(A)` a column for each independent direction `A*x` can take. Both come from the singular value decomposition, so the columns are orthonormal; their numbers add up to the number of `A`'s columns.

examples.title: A singular matrix

pages.summary: The reduced row echelon form, by Gauss-Jordan elimination.
body: Each pivot is 1 with zeros above and below it. For an augmented matrix `[A b]` it shows the solutions of `A*x = b`; the pivot columns `p` (from `[R, p]`) are a basis of the range, and `length(p)` is the rank. For solving systems numerically, `\` is more accurate.

examples.title: A system with a free variable
examples.intro: x + 2y + z = 4, 2x + 4y = 2, 3x + 6y + z = 6. The row of zeros says one equation follows from the others; the rest say x = 1 - 2y and z = 3, for any y.

pages.summary: The matrix exponential, e^A.
body: The sum `I + A + A^2/2! + A^3/3! + ...`, computed by scaling and squaring. The solution of the linear system `x' = A*x` from `x(0)` is `expm(A*t)*x(0)`. Not the same as `exp(A)`, which takes the exponential of each element.

examples.title: Not the elementwise exponential
A damped oscillator, x'' + 0.4x' + 4x = 0

pages.summary: The matrix logarithm and the principal matrix square root.
body: `L = logm(A)` satisfies `expm(L) = A`; `X = sqrtm(A)` satisfies `X*X = A`, the square root whose eigenvalues have positive real parts. Both act on the matrix as a whole, not on each element.

examples.title: Each undoes its inverse

pages.summary: A function of a matrix, from an elementwise function.
body: `funm(A, @cos)` is the matrix cosine: the function applied to the eigenvalues, carried back to the matrix (not `cos` of each element). `funm(A, @exp)` is `expm(A)`.

examples.title: The matrix cosine and exponential
examples.code:
A = [2 1; 1 2];
C = funm(A, @cos)
cos(A)
norm(funm(A, @exp) - expm(A))

pages.summary: The cross product of 3-element vectors.
body: A vector perpendicular to both, whose length is the area of the parallelogram they span; it changes sign when they swap. For matrices, the product of each pair of columns (or along `dim`).

examples.title: Perpendicular, and an area

pages.summary: The dot product.
body: `sum(conj(a).*b)`: for real vectors, the sum of the products of the elements. For matrices, the dot product of each pair of columns (or along `dim`).

examples.title: The angle between two vectors

pages.summary: Solve A*x = b, told what kind of matrix A is.
body: Without options, the same as `\`. With an options struct saying the matrix is upper triangular (`UT`), lower triangular (`LT`), symmetric positive definite (`POSDEF`), symmetric (`SYM`) and so on, the checks are skipped and the right method used directly; `TRANSA` solves `A'*x = b`.

examples.title: An upper triangular system

pages.summary: A matrix balanced to make its eigenvalues more accurate.
body: A diagonal similarity `B = T\A*T` that makes the rows and columns of `B` close in norm. The eigenvalues stay the same, and for a badly scaled matrix they come out more accurately. `T` has powers of 2 on its diagonal (permuted when the matrix has isolated eigenvalues), so balancing adds no rounding.

examples.title: A badly scaled matrix

pages.summary: True when a matrix equals its transpose (or conjugate transpose).
body: With `'skew'`, true when it equals minus it; with `tol`, when it is that close (in the 1-norm sense of `norm(A - A', 1)`). A complex matrix can be Hermitian without being symmetric.

examples.title: Symmetric, skew and Hermitian
examples.code:
issymmetric([1 2; 2 1])
issymmetric([0 1; -1 0], 'skew')
C = [1 1i; -1i 2];
[issymmetric(C) ishermitian(C)]
examples.output:
ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  1×2 logical array

   0   1

examples.title: Close enough
examples.code:
A = [1 2; 2 + 1e-12 1];
[issymmetric(A) issymmetric(A, 1e-10)]

pages.summary: Tests of where a matrix's nonzeros are: below the diagonal, above it, on it, or within a band.
body: `istril` is true when every element above the diagonal is zero, `istriu` below it, `isdiag` both. `bandwidth` gives how far the nonzeros reach below and above the diagonal, and `isbanded(A, lower, upper)` is true when they stay within those numbers of diagonals. For a dynamic system, `bandwidth(sys)` is instead the first frequency where the gain falls 3 dB below its DC gain.
syntax: The band's reach below and above.

examples.title: Triangles and a band
examples.output:
ans =

  1×3 logical array

   1   0   0

lo =

     2

up =

     1

ans =

  1×2 logical array

   1   0

pages.summary: Solve A*x = b by preconditioned conjugate gradients, for a symmetric positive definite A.
body: An iterative method for large sparse systems: each step needs only a product `A*x`, and the residual of a symmetric positive definite system falls until it is within `tol` (1e-6 relative) or `maxit` steps (20) run out. A preconditioner `M = M1*M2` close to `A` but easy to solve with, such as an incomplete Cholesky factor, cuts the number of steps. `A` and the preconditioners may be function handles.
syntax: x = pcg(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)
With a tolerance, a limit on the steps, a preconditioner and a start.
With `flag` (0 converged, 1 out of steps, ...), the relative residual, the steps and the residual at each.

examples.title: With and without a preconditioner

pages.summary: Solve A*x = b by the generalized minimum residual method, with restarts.
body: For any square matrix, symmetric or not: each step adds a direction and takes the `x` with the smallest residual among all those reachable. The directions are stored, so after `restart` of them the method starts again from where it is (no restart by default). `iter` is the outer and inner step.
syntax: x = gmres(A, b, restart, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)
Restarted, with a tolerance, limits, preconditioner and start.
With the flag, relative residual, steps ([outer inner]) and residuals.

examples.title: A nonsymmetric system

pages.summary: Solve A*x = b for a nonsymmetric A by biconjugate gradient methods.
body: Short-recurrence alternatives to `gmres`: each step costs the same however many have been taken, at the price of a residual that need not fall at every step. `bicg` and `qmr` also need products with `A'`; `bicgstab`, `bicgstabl`, `cgs` and `tfqmr` do not. All take `(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)` and return `[x, flag, relres, iter, resvec]`; a function handle for `A` in `bicg` and `qmr` is called as `afun(x, 'notransp')` and `afun(x, 'transp')`.
syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = bicgstab(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)
With the flag, relative residual, steps and residuals; the same for `bicg`, `bicgstabl`, `cgs`, `qmr` and `tfqmr`.

examples.title: The same system, six ways
examples.output:
bicg       flag 0  steps  30.0  residual 6.4e-09
bicgstab   flag 0  steps  15.0  residual 9.2e-09
bicgstabl  flag 0  steps   7.0  residual 9.6e-09
cgs        flag 0  steps  17.0  residual 6.8e-09
qmr        flag 0  steps  29.0  residual 7.2e-09
tfqmr      flag 0  steps  37.0  residual 6.9e-10

pages.summary: Solve A*x = b for a symmetric A, which need not be positive definite.
body: Where `pcg` needs a positive definite matrix, `minres` (smallest residual at each step) and `symmlq` (from the LQ factorization) work for any symmetric one. A preconditioner must be positive definite. Both take `(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)`.
syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = minres(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)
With the flag, relative residual, steps and residuals.
[x, flag, relres, iter] = symmlq(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)

examples.title: A symmetric matrix with negative eigenvalues
examples.output:
minres: flag 0, 15 steps, residual 5.5e-12
symmlq: flag 0, 15 steps, residual 1.1e-11

pages.summary: The least-squares solution of A*x = b by LSQR.
body: For a large sparse (or rectangular) `A`: the iterative counterpart of `A\b` for a tall system, minimizing `norm(b - A*x)`, with products by `A` and `A'` only.
syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = lsqr(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0)
With a tolerance, limits, preconditioner and start, and the flag, residual and steps.

examples.title: A tall system

pages.summary: The Cholesky factor updated after a rank-one change.
body: When `R` is the factor of `A`, `cholupdate(R, x)` is the factor of `A + x*x'`, and `cholupdate(R, x, '-')` of `A - x*x'` (if that is still positive definite; `p` says when it is not). An update takes O(n²) work where factoring again takes O(n³).
syntax: The factor of `A - x*x'`, `p` 0 when it exists.

examples.title: Up and down again

pages.summary: A QR factorization updated after a change of the matrix.
body: When `A = Q*R`: `qrupdate` gives the factors of `A + u*v'`; `qrinsert` of `A` with a column (or, with `'row'`, a row) `x` inserted before position `j`; `qrdelete` of `A` with column (or row) `j` removed. Cheaper than factoring again, as in methods that add and drop variables one at a time.

examples.title: A column in, a column out

pages.summary: Eigenvalues of a matrix polynomial: (A0 + e*A1 + ... + e^p*Ap)*x = 0.
body: The quadratic case comes from vibrations: for `M*x'' + C*x' + K*x = 0`, solutions `x = v*exp(e*t)` need `(K + e*C + e^2*M)*v = 0`, so `polyeig(K, C, M)` gives the modes, damped where the real parts are negative. There are `p*n` eigenvalues for `n`-by-`n` matrices; `s` gives their condition numbers.

examples.title: Two masses on springs, with damping

pages.summary: Plane (Givens) rotations that zero an element.
body: `G = givens(x, y)` is the 2-by-2 rotation with `G*[x; y] = [r; 0]`, `r` the length of `[x; y]`; `planerot` takes the vector and returns the rotated vector too. They are the steps of QR factorizations that zero one element at a time.

examples.title: A 3-4-5 triangle
examples.code:
G = givens(3, 4)
G*[3; 4]
[G, y] = planerot([3; 4])

pages.summary: The generalized singular value decomposition of a pair of matrices.
body: `A = U*C*X'` and `B = V*S*X'` with `U` and `V` unitary, `C` and `S` nonnegative diagonal and `C'*C + S'*S = I`. The generalized singular values `sqrt(diag(C'*C)./diag(S'*S))`, in increasing order, are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the pair `A'*A`, `B'*B`. They appear in regularized least squares (Tikhonov), where `B` is the penalty.
syntax: [U, V, X, C, S] = gsvd(A, B)
[U, V, X, C, S] = gsvd(A, B, 0)

examples.title: The values, and where they come from

pages.summary: Test matrices, by name.
body: Matrices with known properties for trying out algorithms: ill-conditioned (`'lotkin'`, `'kahan'`), with known eigenvalues (`'tridiag'`, `'clement'`), with sensitive eigenvalues (`'grcar'`, `'frank'`), sparse (`'poisson'`, `'tridiag'`, `'wathen'`), random with set properties (`'randsvd'`, `'rando'`), and many more: `binomial`, `cauchy`, `chebspec`, `chebvand`, `chow`, `circul`, `cycol`, `dorr`, `fiedler`, `forsythe`, `gcdmat`, `gearmat`, `hanowa`, `house`, `invhess`, `invol`, `ipjfact`, `jordbloc`, `kms`, `krylov`, `lauchli`, `lehmer`, `leslie`, `lesp`, `minij`, `moler`, `neumann`, `orthog`, `parter`, `pei`, `prolate`, `randhess`, `redheff`, `riemann`, `ris`, `smoke`, `toeppd`, `toeppen`, `triw`, `wilk`, and the data sets `integerdata`, `uniformdata` and `normaldata`.
syntax: The diagonals of a tridiagonal matrix.
A matrix and a right-hand side.

examples.title: A few small ones
examples.code:
gallery('minij', 4)
gallery('lehmer', 4)
full(gallery('tridiag', 4))

examples.title: The eigenvalues of the Grcar matrix
examples.intro: A Toeplitz matrix whose eigenvalues are very sensitive to rounding.

pages.summary: The least-squares solution with the smallest norm.
body: Like `A\b`, it minimizes `norm(A*x - b)`; when `A` is rank deficient there are many such `x`, and `lsqminnorm` returns the shortest (as `pinv(A)*b` does), through a complete orthogonal decomposition. It warns when `A` is rank deficient unless given `'nowarn'`; with `'RegularizationFactor'`, `lambda^2*norm(x)^2` is added to what is minimized.
syntax: With the rank decided by a tolerance.

examples.title: A rank-deficient system

pages.summary: A matrix factored once, to solve with many times.
body: `decomposition` picks a factorization by the matrix (diagonal, triangular, Cholesky, LDL or LU for a square one, QR otherwise), or takes one by name, and keeps it: `dA\b` then solves without factoring again. `dA'` solves with `A'`, and `rcond(dA)`, `rank(dA)` and `isIllConditioned(dA)` ask about the matrix. Solving with an ill-conditioned matrix warns unless `'CheckCondition'` is false.
syntax: The factorization, chosen by the matrix; `x = dA \ b` then solves `A*x = b`.
Whether the matrix is ill conditioned.

examples.title: Factored once, solved twice
examples.output:
dA = 

  decomposition with properties:

    MatrixSize: [3 3]
          Type: 'chol'

  Show all properties

x1 =

    0.1786
    0.2857
    0.6786

x2 =

   -0.0714
    0.2857
   -0.0714

examples.title: Asked whether it is ill conditioned
examples.code:
isIllConditioned(decomposition(magic(4)))
isIllConditioned(decomposition(magic(5)))

pages.summary: The solution of the Sylvester equation A*X + X*B = C.
body: `A` is m-by-m, `B` n-by-n and `C` m-by-n; the solution is unique when `A` and `-B` share no eigenvalue. With `B = A'` it is the Lyapunov equation of control theory.

pages.summary: Weighted or generalized least squares.
body: Minimizes `(b - A*x)'*W*(b - A*x)`, with `W = diag(w)` for weights or `inv(V)` for a covariance matrix `V` of the observations; with neither it is ordinary least squares. The other outputs are the coefficients' standard errors, the weighted mean squared error and their covariance.
syntax: With standard errors, mean squared error and covariance.

pages.summary: The angle between two subspaces.
body: The largest principal angle between the column spaces of `A` and `B`, in radians: 0 when one contains the other, `pi/2` when some direction of one is perpendicular to all of the other.

pages.summary: The condition numbers of the eigenvalues.
body: How much each eigenvalue can move for a small change of the matrix: 1 for every eigenvalue of a symmetric (normal) matrix, large when eigenvectors are nearly parallel.
syntax: The condition number of each eigenvalue.
With the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of `eig`.

examples.title: Normal, and nearly defective
examples.intro: A symmetric matrix's eigenvalues have condition number 1. In the second matrix a change of 1e-6 in one element moves the nearly equal eigenvalues by about 0.006: their condition numbers are near 10^4.

pages.summary: Eigenvalues from complex diagonal form to real block diagonal form.
body: For a real matrix with complex eigenvalues, `eig` gives complex `V` and `D`. `cdf2rdf` turns each conjugate pair `a ± bi` into a 2-by-2 block `[a b; -b a]` and its eigenvectors into their real and imaginary parts, so `A*V = V*D` still holds with real `V` and `D`.

examples.title: A rotation and a stretch

pages.summary: A Hadamard matrix: entries 1 and -1, its columns orthogonal.
body: `H'*H = n*I`. Defined here for `n`, `n/12` or `n/20` a power of 2.

examples.title: Orthogonal columns
examples.code:
H = hadamard(4)
H'*H

pages.summary: The characteristic and minimal polynomials of a matrix, computed exactly.
body: `charpoly` gives the coefficients of `det(x*I - A)`, highest power first; its roots are the eigenvalues. `minpoly` gives the monic polynomial of lowest degree with `p(A) = 0`, which divides it. With a symbolic `x`, the polynomials in `x`.
syntax: As a polynomial in a symbolic `x`.

examples.title: They differ when an eigenvalue repeats
examples.code:
A = 2*eye(3);
charpoly(A)
minpoly(A)
B = [2 1 0; 0 2 0; 0 0 3];
charpoly(B)
minpoly(B)
syms x
charpoly(B, x)

pages.summary: The Jordan form of a matrix, computed exactly.
body: `A*V = V*J` with `J` block diagonal: each block has an eigenvalue on its diagonal and ones just above it, and a block bigger than 1-by-1 means the matrix lacks a full set of eigenvectors. The form is computed in exact arithmetic, since rounding destroys it.
